newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Volume low in second Palestinan bourse session.
newsitem.headline: Volume low in second Palestinan bourse session.

text.p: The embryonic Palestinian stock market ended its second week of trading in the West Bank city of Nablus on Tuesday but said no data would be released until volume picked up in the bourse, now only open one day a week.

"We will not be publishing daily market data during the introductory phase because volume is extremely limited. Demand and supply don't exist, so for the first few weeks market data for turnover would be misleading," said Safwan al-Bataineh, general manager of the Palestinian Securities Exchange.
He said 23 companies were listed on the bourse launched last week and another 20 were in the process of joining.
"At this preliminary period there isn't heavy trading, but what was surprising to some was that most of the orders were buy orders," he told Reuters.

"This means that people have confidence in the companies and in the stock market," said Jiries Qassis, general manager of the United Securities Co, one of four brokerage firms based in Ramallah and Nablus registered to do business at the exchange.
"I believe we have made a good start just one week after the exchange opened. This is a build-up area for bringing accounts and increasing the trading volume," Qassis told Reuters.
Omar Mahmoud, head trader for the Target Securities, said overall there was slight increase in the prices of around 1,000 shares in this week's transactions.
Trading is being conducted in the dinar or the dollar, depending on which currency the company was capitalised.

Bataineh said that during the introductory phase expected to last several weeks, the exchange would hold one weekly trading session. Regular trading, with several sessions per week, would begin as trading volume builds up.
Brokers opened more than 200 accounts for Palestinian investors from across the West Bank and Gaza Strip since the market was launched, Bataineh said.
Brokerage firms said investors from Jordan and Israel had begun making inquiries about investing through the $2 million electronic bourse.

The market was set up to help attract long-term investment from expatriate Palestinians, foreign capital and provide an alternative to common forms of investments such as bank deposits and real estate.
"But all the orders we have are from Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza Strip and one from Jordan. We haven't seen any accounts opened for Israelis," Bataineh said.
